title: glibc: glibc: Denial of Service via memory allocation failure during regular expression processing

vendor.description: The regcomp and regexec functions in the GNU C Library version 2.3 to version 2.44 may read freed memory and free the same heap block twice when a memory allocation fails while a regular expression is compiled or matched.  The re_dfa_add_node (the NFA node table) and build_range_exp (bracket ranges) grow several arrays with consecutive realloc calls and store the new pointers only after all of them succeed.  When a later call fails, the pattern buffer keeps pointers to blocks that were already freed, and the error cleanup frees them again.  In regexec, the back-reference cache (match_ctx_add_entry) frees its array when a realloc fails but keeps the pointer, which is freed again on the error path.  An attacker does not need to supply a crafted regular expression: patterns large enough to grow these arrays are common.  The failure has to hit a specific allocation, though, so the issue can only be reached when the system is already under memory pressure.  An attacker who supplies the pattern or the subject string has little control over which allocation fails, so the expected impact is a crash of the process.  This issue affects all architectures and ABIs supported by the GNU C Library.

title: glibc: glibc: Memory corruption via out-of-bounds write in wide scanf functions

vendor.description: Calling the wide scanf family of functions (swscanf, fwscanf, wscanf, vswscanf, vfwscanf and vwscanf) with a %s or %[ conversion without the 'l' length modifier in the GNU C Library version 2.2 to version 2.44 writes an extra null byte one past the end of the destination array when the converted multibyte string and its terminating null byte exactly fill that array.  These conversions store each wide input character into the caller's char array as a multibyte sequence.  The conversion ends with the sequence that returns to the initial shift state, which also stores the terminating null byte, and the functions then append a second null byte.  A destination sized for the converted string and one terminator, as the C standard requires the caller to provide, is therefore written one byte past its end.  The out-of-bounds byte is always a null byte, which may corrupt adjacent data or crash the process.  An attacker who supplies the input can trigger the overflow with a string whose converted length exactly fills the destination.  The narrow scanf functions, the %ls and %l[ conversions into a wchar_t array, and the 'a' and 'm' allocation modifiers are not affected, and storing a wide scanf conversion into a narrow char array is uncommon.  This issue affects all architectures and ABIs supported by the GNU C Library.

title: glibc: glibc: Denial of Service via out-of-bounds read in CP949 character conversion

vendor.description: Converting crafted CP949 input to UTF-8 character encoding and ignoring invalid characters, in the GNU C Library version 2.1 or later may result in the converter reading past the end of the input buffer, causing the calling application to crash.  When the CP949 decoder encounters an invalid input byte sequence like '\xa2\xe8' it ends up advancing the pointer tracking the read buffer position twice.  If //IGNORE is set on the destination encoding and this sequence is at the end of the input buffer, the decoder may then end up reading past the bounds of the input buffer.  To exploit this, the target iconv function needs to set //IGNORE on the destination of the conversion and the input and encoding needs to be attacker controlled.

title: Converting crafted ISO-2022-CN-EXT input in the GNU C Library version  ...

title: Converting crafted input from UCS-4 to IBM1390 or IBM1399 character en ...

vendor.description: Converting crafted input from UCS-4 to IBM1390 or IBM1399 character encoding, in the GNU C Library version 2.3.3 and later may result in the converter reading past the end of the input buffer, causing the calling application to crash.  When converting from UCS-4, these encoders may encounter a combining base such as U+00E6 and jump ahead by 4 bytes to check the next UCS-4 code point.  The check for end of buffer however does not account for this, which may result in a buffer overread if the following code point has less than 4 bytes remaining.  Exploitation of this bug not only requires attacker control of input and encoding, but also strict control over layout of the input in memory.

title: glibc: glibc: Denial of Service via double free in glob functions

vendor.description: The glob functions in the GNU C Library versions 2.44 and earlier may free the same heap block twice when a memory allocation fails while glob prepends the directory name to the names it matched.  The names already rewritten are freed, but their pointers stay in the result vector, and the error path frees them again with globfree.  The allocation must fail after at least one name has been rewritten, so the issue can only be reached when the process is already close to its memory limit, for example under an address space limit (RLIMIT_AS) or on a 32-bit system.  The attacker needs control to make the result large enough to make the program or service run out of memory, either by controlling the glob pattern and having knowledge of the filesystem layout or through other means.  This issue affects all architectures and ABIs supported by the GNU C Library.

title: glibc: glibc: Heap buffer overflow via attacker-controlled fopen mode string

vendor.description: Passing an effectively empty string to the `,ccs=` syntax extension of the mode argument in the `fopen` function in the GNU C Library version 2.45 or earlier may result in a heap buffer overflow when the mode string input to the function is attacker controlled.    This usage pattern is not seen in applications in common GNU/Linux distributions and applications that process user-supplied values for `ccs` should not pass them through without validation.

title: glibc: Buffer Overflow in strfmon right-justification padding

vendor.description: Calling strfmon and strfmon_l in the GNU C Library version 2.38 to 2.44 can write past the end of the caller-supplied output buffer when a conversion uses right-justified width padding.  Exploitation requires an application code path that calls strfmon or strfmon_l with right-justified width padding into a destination buffer that is large enough for the padding to succeed but too small for the internal memmove call. The field width or format may be attacker-influenced or a fixed susceptible pattern in the caller.  At the time of publication, no network-facing application impact is known.

title: glibc: Fix out-of-bounds array write in tdelete

vendor.description: Calling tdelete on a sufficiently deep tree in the GNU C Library version 2.1 to 2.44 may write one pointer past the end of an alloca-allocated array on the stack, which may crash the application.  The tdelete implementation keeps an explicit stack of parent nodes for rebalancing, which is grown as needed while descending the tree.  Two rebalancing branches push an additional entry without checking the capacity, and write past the array when the stack is exactly full. Triggering this requires a node at a depth of exactly 40 (or 40 plus a multiple of 20), which implies a tree with at least a million nodes, so an attacker must drive a large number of insertions and deletions through an application that uses tsearch and tdelete.  The written value is a pointer into a tree node and is not directly attacker controlled.  No affected application in common distributions has been identified.

title: glibc: glibc: Out-of-bounds write via TSIG record processing

vendor.description: The deprecated functions ns_printrrf, ns_printrr and fp_nquery in the GNU C Library version 2.2 and newer fail to enforce the caller-supplied buffer length, and can result in an out-of-bounds write when printing TSIG records.

title: glibc: glibc: Heap Buffer Overflow in `scanf` with `%mc` format specifier and large width

vendor.description: Calling the scanf family of functions with a %mc (malloc'd character match) in the GNU C Library version 2.7 to version 2.43 with a format width specifier with an explicit width greater than 1024 could result in a one byte heap buffer overflow.

title: glibc: glibc: Information disclosure or denial of service via ungetwc function with specific wide character encodings

vendor.description: Calling the ungetwc function on a FILE stream with wide characters encoded in a character set that has overlaps between its single byte and multi-byte character encodings, in the GNU C Library version 2.43 or earlier, may result in an attempt to read bytes before an allocated buffer, potentially resulting in unintentional disclosure of neighboring data in the heap, or a program crash.  A bug in the wide character pushback implementation (_IO_wdefault_pbackfail in libio/wgenops.c) causes ungetwc() to operate on the regular character buffer (fp->_IO_read_ptr) instead of the actual wide-stream read pointer (fp->_wide_data->_IO_read_ptr). The program crash may happen in cases where fp->_IO_read_ptr is not initialized and hence points to NULL. The buffer under-read requires a special situation where the input character encoding is such that there are overlaps between single byte representations and multibyte representations in that encoding, resulting in spurious matches. The spurious match case is not possible in the standard Unicode character sets.

title: glibc: glibc: Application crash or uninitialized memory read via crafted DNS response

vendor.description: The deprecated functions ns_printrrf, ns_printrr and fp_nquery in the GNU C Library version 2.0.1 to version 2.43 fail to validate the RDATA content against the RDATA length in a DNS response when processing A6, CERT, LOC, TKEY or TSIG records, which may allow an attacker to craft a DNS response, causing a target application to crash or read uninitialized memory.  These functions are for application debugging only and hence not in the path of code executed by the DNS resolver.  Further, they have been deprecated since version 2.34 and should not be used by any new applications.  Applications should consider porting away from these interfaces since they may be removed in future versions.

title: glibc: glibc: Process abort due to invalid memory in wordexp

vendor.description: Calling wordexp with WRDE_APPEND in the GNU C Library version 2.0 to version 2.43 can cause the interface to return invalid memory in the we_wordv member, which on subsequent calls to wordfree may abort the process.

title: glibc: Glibc: Denial of Service via stack exhaustion during tilde expansion

vendor.description: When expanding paths that begin with a tilde (~) followed by a username, the internal parse_tilde function extracts the username to determine the user's home directory.  The implementation allocates memory for this username directly on the stack using the strndupa macro. Because the size of this allocation was determined by the length of the user-supplied input without any bounds checks, passing an excessively long username e.g. thousands of characters, forces the thread to exhaust its stack space. Thus if an application passes untrusted, attacker-controlled input to the wordexp function, an attacker can trigger a stack clash.

title: glibc: Non-progress DoS in SHIFT_JISX0213 -&gt

vendor.description: Converting crafted SHIFT_JISX0213 input to UCS-4 or the internal wide character encoding, for example with iconv, in the GNU C Library version 2.3 to 2.44 may result in the converter making no progress, causing the calling application to hang.  Some SHIFT_JISX0213 sequences decode to two code points.  If the output buffer has room for only the first one, the converter stores the second in the conversion state and returns E2BIG, but it never clears that pending character after emitting it on the next call.  The converter then keeps emitting the pending character without consuming further input, so an application that retries the conversion loops forever. The input must be attacker controlled and the application must convert it with an output buffer small enough to split the two code points. Only the SHIFT_JISX0213 character set is affected, which is not commonly used.  The related defect in the EUC_JISX0213 converter is tracked separately as CVE-2026-80489.

title: glibc: glibc: Arbitrary code execution via directory traversal in LANGUAGE environment variable

vendor.description: The gettext family of functions in the GNU C Library version 2.0 and later accept LANGUAGE environment variable entries that contain '/' or that are equal to "..", unless the program is setuid or setgid (AT_SECURE).  An attacker who can set LANGUAGE in the environment of a program that uses gettext can make it load a message catalog (.mo file) from an arbitrary location in the file system.  A crafted .mo file can crash the program through out-of-range offsets, or supply translations whose format directives do not match the arguments passed by the program.  That causes undefined behaviour in the printf family of functions and may allow arbitrary code execution with the privileges of the program.  The safety of message catalogs relies on them being installed in trusted, read-only locations, and the directory traversal bypasses this.  The fix for CVE-2014-0475 rejects ".." path components in locale names passed to setlocale or taken from the LC_ALL, LC_* and LANG environment variables.  gettext reads LANGUAGE directly and appends each colon-separated entry to the message catalog directory, so that fix did not cover LANGUAGE.  LANGUAGE is only used when the LC_MESSAGES locale is not "C", "C.<encoding>" or "POSIX", so the attacker must also be able to select another installed locale, for example through LANG or LC_ALL.  Exploitation also requires that the attacker can place the crafted file in a location readable by the target program, and that the environment crosses a trust boundary without the program running as AT_SECURE.  An example is an SSH server that accepts LANGUAGE and LANG from clients through the AcceptEnv directive and restricts an account to a forced command; the attacker may use this to escape the restriction.

title: glibc: glibc DNS stub resolver: Denial of Service via long search domain in configuration

vendor.description: Initializing the DNS stub resolver from an /etc/resolv.conf file, or a LOCALDOMAIN environment variable, whose search list contains a domain of roughly 200 characters or more in the GNU C Library version 2.26 to 2.44 results in an assertion failure which aborts the process.  The resolver truncates the search list when copying it into the fixed-size _res.defdname buffer, then asserts that the copy is consistent with the full configuration.  The consistency check compared against the wrong size and did not handle a first entry that does not fit, so a correctly truncated list failed the assertion.  Any process that resolves names through the library is affected, including long-running processes that reload /etc/resolv.conf on the next query after it changes.  Search domains are commonly written to /etc/resolv.conf from data received over DHCP or from a VPN server, so an attacker on the local network may be able to trigger this without privileges on the target system, subject to validation by the network configuration software.

title: glibc: glibc: Privilege escalation and arbitrary code execution via TOCTOU race condition in dynamic loader

vendor.description: A time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) race condition in the dynamic loader (ld.so) of the GNU C Library (glibc) versions 2.14 through 2.44 allows a local attacker to escalate privileges. When expanding $ORIGIN in DT_RPATH for setuid/setgid (AT_SECURE) programs, glibc validates the lexically normalized search path against the trusted directories but then opens the raw, un-normalized path. On systems where the Linux fs.protected_hardlinks sysctl is disabled, a local attacker who hard-links such a program into an attacker-controlled directory and wins a race to replace an intermediate path component with a symbolic link can direct the loader outside the trusted directory, causing it to load an attacker-controlled shared object and execute arbitrary code with the elevated privileges of the program.  Exploitation requires an installed setuid or setgid binary whose DT_RPATH uses $ORIGIN followed by ".." traversal that normalizes into a trusted directory, and the ability to hard-link that binary and win the race by swapping a path component for a symbolic link. Major Linux-based OS distributions ship with fs.protected_hardlinks enabled by default and mitigate the vulnerability.

title: glibc: nscd stack overflow leads to degraded DNS resolution

vendor.description: The nscd service in the GNU C Library 2.3.4 onwards may crash due to a  stack overflow when a malicious DNS server returns too large a response  for a DNS query, resulting in degraded DNS resolution for the system.    Exploitation of this bug needs a system that has nscd enabled and using  an untrusted DNS server for name resolution, with the compromised DNS  server being capable of processing records large enough to result in a  stack overflow in an nscd thread stack.  During experimentation, bind 9  was unable to handle large records, but that could change in future or  with a different name server.  In typical installations, nscd is  executed in an isolated context as its own user without a shell, due to  which any compromise of that service is isolated.    There is a remote possibility of nscd cache corruption if an attacker  manages to get the stack pointer into a desired point in the heap,  potentially resulting in other caches in nscd being overwritten with  corrupt data through the stack overflow, until the buggy code path  eventually results in a crash.    Finally, a crash in nscd may result in performance degradation when  resolving names, but it does not result in a denial of service.

title: glibc: glibc: Local attacker can cause denial of service and information disclosure via stack-based buffer overflow.

vendor.description: A stack-based buffer overflow in the dynamic loader (ld.so) of the GNU C Library (glibc) versions 2.14 through 2.44 allows a local attacker to crash or corrupt the memory of setuid/setgid (AT_SECURE) programs.  When such a program's DT_RPATH or DT_RUNPATH begins with $ORIGIN and is followed by NUL or '/' the loader both reads past the end of the path buffer and writes past the end of a stack-allocated internal buffer. title: glibc: glibc: Denial of Service via out-of-bounds read in strncasecmp

title: gzip: gzip: Arbitrary file overwrite via insecure temporary file handling in gzexe utility

vendor.description: GNU gzip contains a vulnerability in the gzexe utility related to insecure temporary file handling. title: gzip: gzip: Information disclosure via global buffer overflow in LZH decompression

title: openssl: openssl: Denial of Service via malformed PEM data in PEM_X509_INFO_read_bio_ex

vendor.description: Issue summary: When an application passes a stack to PEM_X509_INFO_read_bio_ex() to add entries to, and reading fails, OpenSSL frees every entry in the stack, both the old ones and any new ones, but leaves them in the stack.  Impact summary: An application that passes an existing stack to PEM_X509_INFO_read_bio_ex() and keeps using it after a failed read may use memory that was already freed. This can cause a crash or, in principle, memory corruption. Malformed PEM data can make the read fail, but only applications that pass an existing stack are affected, and OpenSSL itself does not do this.  CWE: CWE-416: Use After Free  Description: PEM_X509_INFO_read_bio_ex() reads certificates, CRLs and private keys from PEM data and adds them to a stack of X509_INFO structures. If the application passes a stack that is not NULL, the function adds the new entries to it and must leave the entries that are already there unchanged.  If reading fails, the function frees every entry in the stack. This includes the entries that were there before the call, and the entries added by the call. It does not remove these entries from the stack, so the stack keeps pointers to freed memory. The failure can happen at any point, even before any entry was added. A PEM item with invalid content is enough.  This also happens if the stack was empty: entries added before the failure are freed but stay in the stack.  An application that then reads or frees the stack will use memory that was already freed. This can crash the application or, in principle, corrupt memory.  Only applications that pass a stack that is not NULL are affected. OpenSSL itself never does this. Its own callers, including the code that TLS uses to load CA certificates, always pass NULL. When the stack is NULL, the function frees only the entries that it created itself, which is safe. We expect that very few applications pass an existing stack. An attacker can make the read fail with malformed PEM data, but cannot make an application pass an existing stack.  The same problem affects PEM_X509_INFO_read_bio(), PEM_X509_INFO_read() and PEM_X509_INFO_read_ex(), which use the same code. OpenSSL 1.1.1 and 1.0.2 have only the first two of these functions.  FIPS impact: no The affected code is outside the FIPS module boundary.

title: openssl: openssl: Denial of Service via crafted EC certificate in CMS encryption

vendor.description: Issue summary: Encrypting a CMS message to an EC certificate whose group order is 1 may cause CMS_encrypt() or CMS_encrypt_ex() to loop indefinitely.  Impact summary: An attacker able to supply the recipient certificate to an application performing CMS encryption can cause that application to loop indefinitely, consuming CPU and resulting in Denial of Service.  CWE: CWE-835: Loop with Unreachable Exit Condition ('Infinite Loop')  Description: CMS_encrypt() and CMS_encrypt_ex() encrypt a message to one or more recipient certificates and, for an EC recipient, generate an ephemeral key in the recipient's group. If the certificate declares a group order of 1, random scalar generation can only produce zero. The key generation routine then retries without limit while waiting for a nonzero private scalar, so the call never returns.  The OpenSSL TLS and QUIC implementations do not use this path. An application is exposed only if it calls CMS_encrypt() or CMS_encrypt_ex() with a recipient certificate whose EC parameters are attacker-controlled. Certificates with normal EC group orders do not trigger the loop.  OpenSSL 4.0 and later reject unknown explicit EC groups in default builds. These versions are affected only when configured with the enable-ec_explicit_curves option.  The result is a hang that consumes a CPU core until the process is interrupted, a Denial of Service. The severity is Low because the attacker must supply the recipient certificate and the application must choose to encrypt to it; ordinary CMS encryption to trusted recipients is unaffected.  The fix makes EC key generation fail when the group has no valid nonzero private scalar, instead of retrying indefinitely.  FIPS impact: no The FIPS modules in 4.1, 4.0, 3.5 and 3.0 are not affected. The FIPS provider does not support arbitrary explicit EC domain parameters, so an order-1 group is rejected during key import before the vulnerable key generation path is reached.

title: openssl: openssl: Out-of-bounds write via integer overflow in EVP_EncodeBlock()

vendor.description: Issue summary: Calling EVP_EncodeBlock() with an input length close to INT_MAX may overflow the calculation of the encoded output size and write past the end of the caller-supplied output buffer.  Impact summary: No path by which an attacker can trigger this has been identified. An application that passes an input length near INT_MAX to EVP_EncodeBlock() could suffer a heap buffer overflow, crashing or corrupting its own memory, but it must itself supply such a length.  CWE: CWE-190: Integer Overflow or Wraparound  Description: EVP_EncodeBlock() base64-encodes a buffer of a caller-supplied length into an output buffer that the caller allocates. The caller is expected to reserve 4*((len+2)/3)+1 bytes. For input lengths close to INT_MAX, the arithmetic that computes the encoded length overflows a signed integer, so the function writes more data than the documented output size. The result is a heap buffer overflow in the calling process.  Reaching this requires an application to pass an input length near INT_MAX to EVP_EncodeBlock(). OpenSSL's TLS, QUIC and CMS implementations never encode buffers of that size, and the command line tools cannot practically be made to do so: the limits on reading a proxy password from a file and on bignum sizes prevent it. An application that accepts an attacker-controlled length and forwards it to EVP_EncodeBlock() without its own bound check is exposed.  The severity is Low because no attacker-controlled path to the overflow is known. The caller must already hold a buffer of about two gigabytes before the defect can be reached.  FIPS impact: no The affected code is outside the FIPS module boundary.

title: openssl: OpenSSL: Denial of Service via NULL pointer dereference during DANE TLSA record processing

vendor.description: Issue summary: A DANE-enabled TLS client may crash by dereferencing a NULL pointer when processing an unusual combination of certificate and TLSA records.  Impact summary: The impact is limited to a client crash (potential Denial of Service).  CWE: CWE-476: NULL Pointer Dereference  Description: A DANE-enabled TLS client that supports TLSA records with at least one of the PKIX-TA(0) or PKIX-EE(1) usages alongside the DANE-TA(2) usage may crash by dereferencing a NULL pointer if the server claims a trusted CA's certificate to be its end-entity certificate and has an unusual mix of associated TLSA records.  DANE SMTP clients should not be affected since only the DANE-TA(2) and DANE-EE(3) TLSA record usages are specified applicable in SMTP.  For example, the Postfix MTA is not affected, while the Exim MTA does not at present use OpenSSL's DANE implementation.  Use of DANE in validation of RFC7250 raw public keys (RPKs) is also unaffected, as these only use DANE-EE(3) TLSA records.  Only applications that support combining the DANE PKI with a traditional PKI are potentially affected.  A DANE-enabled browser or similar, that uses OpenSSL's DANE API could be affected.  FIPS impact: no The DANE API is outside the FIPS module boundary.

title: openssl: openssl: Denial of service via crafted out-of-sequence DTLS handshake fragments

vendor.description: Issue summary: Receiving crafted out-of-sequence DTLS handshake fragments may cause OpenSSL to allocate a full message-length reassembly buffer for each buffered message, so a small amount of wire data consumes a large amount of memory.  Impact summary: A remote attacker can send a few small crafted DTLS handshake fragments to make a DTLS server or client allocate well over a megabyte of memory per connection, which may lead to memory exhaustion and Denial of Service if many connections are made.  CWE: CWE-770: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling  Description: DTLS handshake messages can arrive out of order and fragmented, so OpenSSL buffers fragments of up to ten out-of-sequence messages until reassembly is possible. When the first fragment of a new message arrives, OpenSSL allocates a buffer sized to the full message length declared in the fragment header, plus a reassembly bitmap, instead of storing only the bytes actually received. The declared length is capped by the maximum certificate list size, 128KB by default, and that cap applies to every handshake message type rather than only to Certificate messages.  Only DTLS endpoints reach this code. TLS, QUIC and applications that do not use DTLS are unaffected. An attacker sends fragments that declare a large message length but carry almost no data, using up to ten distinct message sequence numbers.  A single connection can then hold roughly 1.4MB of buffers from about 156 bytes on the wire. Because the number of buffered messages is capped, memory exhaustion requires many connections or many peers, which is why the severity is Low.  FIPS impact: no The affected code is outside the FIPS module boundary.

vendor.description: Perl versions through 5.45.1 have out-of-bounds heap reads and writes during regular expression matching via an undersized superlinear cache in S_regmatch.  The regex engine's superlinear cache holds one bit per subject position for each participating WHILEM node, so the bit count is the subject length plus one times the number of nodes. Nothing checks that product for positive overflow of the signed 32-bit count: a 286331153 byte subject matched against a pattern with 15 participating nodes stores the count as 14, leaving a two byte cache. The cache is then indexed from the real match position and node number, so reads go past the end of the allocation, and on failure CACHEsayNO sets a bit past it.  A caller that matches an attacker controlled subject of this size against a pattern of this shape can crash the process or corrupt heap memory.

title: sqlite: SQLite: Arbitrary code execution via crafted FTS5 full-text search data

vendor.description: SQLite before 3.53.2 contains an out-of-bounds read vulnerability in the FTS5 full-text search extension that allows attackers to crash the process by supplying a crafted database with a malformed FTS5 leaf page. Attackers can set an oversized term length in the leaf page so that fts5LeafSeek() reads past the end of the page buffer while comparing terms during an FTS5 MATCH query, in applications compiled with SQLITE_ENABLE_FTS5.

title: sqlite: SQLite: Arbitrary code execution and crash via heap-based buffer overflow in FTS5

vendor.description: SQLite before 3.53.2 contains a heap-based buffer overflow vulnerability in the FTS5 full-text search extension that allows attackers to cause a crash or execute arbitrary code by supplying a crafted database with malicious continuation page metadata specifying a szLeaf value smaller than 4. Attackers can trigger an integer underflow in fts5ChunkIterate() causing an inflated remaining byte count during FTS5 MATCH query processing, leading to a heap buffer overflow of attacker-controlled data in applications compiled with SQLITE_ENABLE_FTS5.

title: sqlite: sqlite: Denial of Service via stack exhaustion from deeply nested Common Table Expressions

vendor.description: SQLite before 3.54.0 contains a stack exhaustion vulnerability that allows attackers to bypass the SQLITE_LIMIT_EXPR_DEPTH nesting limit because common table expressions are not counted against it. Attackers can supply a WITH clause chaining tens of thousands of CTEs, via plain SQL or a view in an untrusted database file, causing unbounded selectExpander() recursion that crashes the process.

title: sqlite: sqlite: Denial of Service via use-after-free in full-text search

title: sqlite: sqlite: Denial of service via heap-based buffer overflow in FTS5

vendor.description: SQLite before 3.54.0 built with FTS5 contains a heap buffer overflow in fts5MergeRowidLists() that undersizes the output buffer when merging detail=none prefix doclists. title: sqlite: sqlite: Arbitrary code execution via corrupted FTS5 index

title: sqlite: sqlite: Information disclosure via undersized WAL page size

title: sqlite: sqlite: Denial of Service via stack exhaustion from chained COLLATE operators

title: tar: tar: TOCTOU in incremental dumpdir 'X' rename handling allows restore path escape

vendor.description: A TOCTOU (Time-of-Check Time-of-Use) vulnerability in GNU tar's incremental dumpdir 'X' rename handling allows a local attacker with write access to a directory being backed up to influence the restore process if the attacker has access to the system where the restore is being performed. During restoration, files or directories may be created, renamed or overwritten outside the intended extraction directory. This could lead to unauthorized file modification or, in some cases, privilege escalation. Exploitation does not require the attacker to modify or craft the archive, and standard backup and restore workflows—including extracting into a newly created directory without using the -P option do not mitigate the issue.

title: tar: tar: --one-top-level hardlink targets not confined to top-level directory enabling arbitrary file overwrite

vendor.description: A flaw was found in the util-linux chfn and chsh utilities when compiled with Readline support. The Readline library uses an "INPUTRC" environment variable to get a path to the library config file. When the library cannot parse the specified file, it prints an error message containing data from the file. This flaw allows an unprivileged user to read root-owned files, potentially leading to privilege escalation. This flaw affects util-linux versions prior to 2.37.4.

title: util-linux: util-linux: heap use-after-free in libblkid nested partition probing

vendor.description: A flaw was found in the libblkid library of util-linux. During nested partition probing, the BSD, Minix, Solaris x86, and UnixWare partition probers cache a raw pointer to a parent partition entry in a dynamically allocated array. When subsequent partition additions cause the array to be reallocated, this pointer becomes stale, leading to a heap use-after-free read. An attacker who can present a crafted block device image (for example, via USB insertion or a loop-mounted disk image) can trigger this flaw without user interaction, as libblkid is invoked automatically by udev/udisks as root on block-device hot-plug events. This could lead to limited information disclosure or denial of service.

title: util-linux: TOCTOU in the mount program when setting up loop devices

vendor.description: util-linux is a random collection of Linux utilities. Prior to version 2.41.4, a TOCTOU (Time-of-Check-Time-of-Use) vulnerability has been identified in the SUID binary /usr/bin/mount from util-linux. The mount binary, when setting up loop devices, validates the source file path with user privileges via fork() + setuid() + realpath(), but subsequently re-canonicalizes and opens it with root privileges (euid=0) without verifying that the path has not been replaced between both operations. Neither O_NOFOLLOW, nor inode comparison, nor post-open fstat() are employed. This allows a local unprivileged user to replace the source file with a symlink pointing to any root-owned file or device during the race window, causing the SUID binary to open and mount it as root. Exploitation requires an /etc/fstab entry with user,loop options whose path points to a directory where the attacker has write permission, and that /usr/bin/mount has the SUID bit set (the default configuration on virtually all Linux distributions). The impact is unauthorized read access to root-protected files and block devices, including backup images, disk volumes, and any file containing a valid filesystem. This issue has been patched in version 2.41.4.

title: util-linux: util-linux: Access control bypass due to improper hostname canonicalization

vendor.description: A flaw was found in util-linux. Improper hostname canonicalization in the `login(1)` utility, when invoked with the `-h` option, can modify the supplied remote hostname before setting `PAM_RHOST`. A remote attacker could exploit this by providing a specially crafted hostname, potentially bypassing host-based Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) access control rules that rely on fully qualified domain names. This could lead to unauthorized access.

title: util-linux: TOCTOU in the mount program via ancestor directory swap on target path

vendor.description: util-linux is a random collection of Linux utilities. In util-linux 2.17 through 2.41.6 and 2.42 through 2.42.3, and in 2.42.4 when the legacy `mount(2)` path is used without `/proc`, restricted non-root `mount` requests validate an `/etc/fstab` target before the mount operation re-resolves that pathname. A local low-privileged user authorized by an fstab `user` or `users` entry whose target has an attacker-writable ancestor can use `renameat2(RENAME_EXCHANGE)` to swap a path component and redirect an authorized mount to a root-owned location, such as mounting attacker-controlled content over `/etc/sudoers.d`, and thereby gain root privileges. Versions 2.41.5 and 2.42.2 pin targets for the new mount API, and 2.42.4 pins legacy targets through `/proc/self/fd`; the documented legacy fallback without `/proc` remains affected.

title: util-linux: util-linux: Partition metadata compromise via integer overflow in DOS partition parser

vendor.description: util-linux is a random collection of Linux utilities. Before util-linux 2.41.4, `parse_dos_extended()` in `libblkid/src/partitions/dos.c` computes an extended-partition start sector with 32-bit addition and does not apply the extended-area bounds checks to the first two EBR entries. A local attacker who causes a crafted DOS extended-partition disk image or removable medium to be probed can wrap `cur_start + start` to sector zero and cause libblkid to report a false partition overlapping the MBR. This directly compromises the integrity of the reported partition metadata; disk modification or availability loss requires a separate downstream consumer to act on that metadata. This issue is fixed in 2.41.4.

title: util-linux: util-linux: restricted bind mounts do not pin the source, allowing X-mount.owner/group/mode redirection

vendor.description: A flaw was found in util-linux. Restricted bind mounts take the source path from fstab but do not pin that source before the privileged mount. A local unprivileged user who can replace the authorized source or a writable ancestor can redirect SUID mount(8) to bind another host directory. If the fstab entry also sets X-mount.owner, X-mount.group, or X-mount.mode, root then changes ownership or mode on that redirected inode.

title: glibc: glibc: Denial of Service via memory allocation failure during regular expression processing

vendor.description: The regcomp and regexec functions in the GNU C Library version 2.3 to version 2.44 may read freed memory and free the same heap block twice when a memory allocation fails while a regular expression is compiled or matched.  The re_dfa_add_node (the NFA node table) and build_range_exp (bracket ranges) grow several arrays with consecutive realloc calls and store the new pointers only after all of them succeed.  When a later call fails, the pattern buffer keeps pointers to blocks that were already freed, and the error cleanup frees them again.  In regexec, the back-reference cache (match_ctx_add_entry) frees its array when a realloc fails but keeps the pointer, which is freed again on the error path.  An attacker does not need to supply a crafted regular expression: patterns large enough to grow these arrays are common.  The failure has to hit a specific allocation, though, so the issue can only be reached when the system is already under memory pressure.  An attacker who supplies the pattern or the subject string has little control over which allocation fails, so the expected impact is a crash of the process.  This issue affects all architectures and ABIs supported by the GNU C Library.

title: glibc: glibc: Memory corruption via out-of-bounds write in wide scanf functions

vendor.description: Calling the wide scanf family of functions (swscanf, fwscanf, wscanf, vswscanf, vfwscanf and vwscanf) with a %s or %[ conversion without the 'l' length modifier in the GNU C Library version 2.2 to version 2.44 writes an extra null byte one past the end of the destination array when the converted multibyte string and its terminating null byte exactly fill that array.  These conversions store each wide input character into the caller's char array as a multibyte sequence.  The conversion ends with the sequence that returns to the initial shift state, which also stores the terminating null byte, and the functions then append a second null byte.  A destination sized for the converted string and one terminator, as the C standard requires the caller to provide, is therefore written one byte past its end.  The out-of-bounds byte is always a null byte, which may corrupt adjacent data or crash the process.  An attacker who supplies the input can trigger the overflow with a string whose converted length exactly fills the destination.  The narrow scanf functions, the %ls and %l[ conversions into a wchar_t array, and the 'a' and 'm' allocation modifiers are not affected, and storing a wide scanf conversion into a narrow char array is uncommon.  This issue affects all architectures and ABIs supported by the GNU C Library.

title: glibc: glibc: Denial of Service via out-of-bounds read in CP949 character conversion

vendor.description: Converting crafted CP949 input to UTF-8 character encoding and ignoring invalid characters, in the GNU C Library version 2.1 or later may result in the converter reading past the end of the input buffer, causing the calling application to crash.  When the CP949 decoder encounters an invalid input byte sequence like '\xa2\xe8' it ends up advancing the pointer tracking the read buffer position twice.  If //IGNORE is set on the destination encoding and this sequence is at the end of the input buffer, the decoder may then end up reading past the bounds of the input buffer.  To exploit this, the target iconv function needs to set //IGNORE on the destination of the conversion and the input and encoding needs to be attacker controlled.

title: Converting crafted input from UCS-4 to IBM1390 or IBM1399 character en ...

vendor.description: Converting crafted input from UCS-4 to IBM1390 or IBM1399 character encoding, in the GNU C Library version 2.3.3 and later may result in the converter reading past the end of the input buffer, causing the calling application to crash. The check for end of buffer however does not account for this, which may result in a buffer overread if the following code point has less than 4 bytes remaining.  Exploitation of this bug not only requires attacker control of input and encoding, but also strict control over layout of the input in memory.

title: glibc: glibc: Denial of Service via double free in glob functions

vendor.description: The glob functions in the GNU C Library versions 2.44 and earlier may free the same heap block twice when a memory allocation fails while glob prepends the directory name to the names it matched.  The names already rewritten are freed, but their pointers stay in the result vector, and the error path frees them again with globfree.  The allocation must fail after at least one name has been rewritten, so the issue can only be reached when the process is already close to its memory limit, for example under an address space limit (RLIMIT_AS) or on a 32-bit system.  The attacker needs control to make the result large enough to make the program or service run out of memory, either by controlling the glob pattern and having knowledge of the filesystem layout or through other means.  This issue affects all architectures and ABIs supported by the GNU C Library.

title: glibc: glibc: Arbitrary code execution via directory traversal in LANGUAGE environment variable

vendor.description: The gettext family of functions in the GNU C Library version 2.0 and later accept LANGUAGE environment variable entries that contain '/' or that are equal to "..", unless the program is setuid or setgid (AT_SECURE).  An attacker who can set LANGUAGE in the environment of a program that uses gettext can make it load a message catalog (.mo file) from an arbitrary location in the file system.  A crafted .mo file can crash the program through out-of-range offsets, or supply translations whose format directives do not match the arguments passed by the program.  That causes undefined behaviour in the printf family of functions and may allow arbitrary code execution with the privileges of the program.  The safety of message catalogs relies on them being installed in trusted, read-only locations, and the directory traversal bypasses this.  The fix for CVE-2014-0475 rejects ".." path components in locale names passed to setlocale or taken from the LC_ALL, LC_* and LANG environment variables.  gettext reads LANGUAGE directly and appends each colon-separated entry to the message catalog directory, so that fix did not cover LANGUAGE.  LANGUAGE is only used when the LC_MESSAGES locale is not "C", "C.<encoding>" or "POSIX", so the attacker must also be able to select another installed locale, for example through LANG or LC_ALL.  Exploitation also requires that the attacker can place the crafted file in a location readable by the target program, and that the environment crosses a trust boundary without the program running as AT_SECURE.  An example is an SSH server that accepts LANGUAGE and LANG from clients through the AcceptEnv directive and restricts an account to a forced command; the attacker may use this to escape the restriction.

title: openssl: openssl: Denial of Service via malformed PEM data in PEM_X509_INFO_read_bio_ex

vendor.description: Issue summary: When an application passes a stack to PEM_X509_INFO_read_bio_ex() to add entries to, and reading fails, OpenSSL frees every entry in the stack, both the old ones and any new ones, but leaves them in the stack.  Impact summary: An application that passes an existing stack to PEM_X509_INFO_read_bio_ex() and keeps using it after a failed read may use memory that was already freed. This can cause a crash or, in principle, memory corruption. Malformed PEM data can make the read fail, but only applications that pass an existing stack are affected, and OpenSSL itself does not do this.  CWE: CWE-416: Use After Free  Description: PEM_X509_INFO_read_bio_ex() reads certificates, CRLs and private keys from PEM data and adds them to a stack of X509_INFO structures. If the application passes a stack that is not NULL, the function adds the new entries to it and must leave the entries that are already there unchanged.  If reading fails, the function frees every entry in the stack. This includes the entries that were there before the call, and the entries added by the call. It does not remove these entries from the stack, so the stack keeps pointers to freed memory. The failure can happen at any point, even before any entry was added. A PEM item with invalid content is enough.  This also happens if the stack was empty: entries added before the failure are freed but stay in the stack.  An application that then reads or frees the stack will use memory that was already freed. This can crash the application or, in principle, corrupt memory.  Only applications that pass a stack that is not NULL are affected. OpenSSL itself never does this. Its own callers, including the code that TLS uses to load CA certificates, always pass NULL. When the stack is NULL, the function frees only the entries that it created itself, which is safe. We expect that very few applications pass an existing stack. An attacker can make the read fail with malformed PEM data, but cannot make an application pass an existing stack.  The same problem affects PEM_X509_INFO_read_bio(), PEM_X509_INFO_read() and PEM_X509_INFO_read_ex(), which use the same code. OpenSSL 1.1.1 and 1.0.2 have only the first two of these functions.  FIPS impact: no The affected code is outside the FIPS module boundary.

title: openssl: OpenSSL: Denial of Service via unbounded QUIC frame queueing

vendor.description: Issue summary: The QUIC stack queues a RETIRE_CONNECTION_ID frame also for retransmitted NEW_CONNECTION_ID frames. This allows a remote malicious QUIC stack to queue an unlimited number of RETIRE_CONNECTION_ID frames.  Impact summary: A malicious remote QUIC peer can trigger an out-of-memory condition causing a Denial of Service.  CWE: CWE-770: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling  Description: The earlier fix for CVE-2026-84784 was not complete. It failed to ignore retransmissions of the NEW_CONNECTION_ID frame. The QUIC implementation created and inserted a RETIRE_CONNECTION_ID frame for every retransmitted NEW_CONNECTION_ID frame it received and there was no limit on how many RETIRE_CONNECTION_ID frames were queued.  This issue allows a malicious remote QUIC stack to trigger an unbounded allocation of memory and eventually an out-of-memory (OOM) condition.  FIPS impact: no The FIPS module is not affected as the QUIC implementation is outside the OpenSSL FIPS module boundary.

title: openssl: openssl: Denial of Service via crafted EC certificate in CMS encryption

vendor.description: Issue summary: Encrypting a CMS message to an EC certificate whose group order is 1 may cause CMS_encrypt() or CMS_encrypt_ex() to loop indefinitely.  Impact summary: An attacker able to supply the recipient certificate to an application performing CMS encryption can cause that application to loop indefinitely, consuming CPU and resulting in Denial of Service.  CWE: CWE-835: Loop with Unreachable Exit Condition ('Infinite Loop')  Description: CMS_encrypt() and CMS_encrypt_ex() encrypt a message to one or more recipient certificates and, for an EC recipient, generate an ephemeral key in the recipient's group. If the certificate declares a group order of 1, random scalar generation can only produce zero. The key generation routine then retries without limit while waiting for a nonzero private scalar, so the call never returns.  The OpenSSL TLS and QUIC implementations do not use this path. An application is exposed only if it calls CMS_encrypt() or CMS_encrypt_ex() with a recipient certificate whose EC parameters are attacker-controlled. Certificates with normal EC group orders do not trigger the loop.  OpenSSL 4.0 and later reject unknown explicit EC groups in default builds. These versions are affected only when configured with the enable-ec_explicit_curves option.  The result is a hang that consumes a CPU core until the process is interrupted, a Denial of Service. The severity is Low because the attacker must supply the recipient certificate and the application must choose to encrypt to it; ordinary CMS encryption to trusted recipients is unaffected.  The fix makes EC key generation fail when the group has no valid nonzero private scalar, instead of retrying indefinitely.  FIPS impact: no The FIPS modules in 4.1, 4.0, 3.5 and 3.0 are not affected. The FIPS provider does not support arbitrary explicit EC domain parameters, so an order-1 group is rejected during key import before the vulnerable key generation path is reached.

title: openssl: openssl: Out-of-bounds write via integer overflow in EVP_EncodeBlock()

vendor.description: Issue summary: Calling EVP_EncodeBlock() with an input length close to INT_MAX may overflow the calculation of the encoded output size and write past the end of the caller-supplied output buffer.  Impact summary: No path by which an attacker can trigger this has been identified. An application that passes an input length near INT_MAX to EVP_EncodeBlock() could suffer a heap buffer overflow, crashing or corrupting its own memory, but it must itself supply such a length.  CWE: CWE-190: Integer Overflow or Wraparound  Description: EVP_EncodeBlock() base64-encodes a buffer of a caller-supplied length into an output buffer that the caller allocates. The caller is expected to reserve 4*((len+2)/3)+1 bytes. For input lengths close to INT_MAX, the arithmetic that computes the encoded length overflows a signed integer, so the function writes more data than the documented output size. The result is a heap buffer overflow in the calling process.  Reaching this requires an application to pass an input length near INT_MAX to EVP_EncodeBlock(). OpenSSL's TLS, QUIC and CMS implementations never encode buffers of that size, and the command line tools cannot practically be made to do so: the limits on reading a proxy password from a file and on bignum sizes prevent it. An application that accepts an attacker-controlled length and forwards it to EVP_EncodeBlock() without its own bound check is exposed.  The severity is Low because no attacker-controlled path to the overflow is known. The caller must already hold a buffer of about two gigabytes before the defect can be reached.  FIPS impact: no The affected code is outside the FIPS module boundary.

title: openssl: openssl: Denial of Service via crafted CMS or PKCS#7 SignedData message

vendor.description: Issue summary: Verifying a maliciously crafted CMS or PKCS#7 SignedData message with CRL checking enabled may consume excessive CPU time, growing with the square of the message size.  Impact summary: An attacker who can submit a CMS or PKCS#7 SignedData message to an application that verifies it with CRL checking enabled can occupy a CPU core for seconds to minutes, causing Denial of Service. Applications that leave CRL checking disabled are not affected.  CWE: CWE-407: Inefficient Algorithmic Complexity  Description: With CRL checking enabled, OpenSSL compares each CRL distribution point of a certificate against the issuing distribution point of every candidate CRL. For a nameRelativeToCRLIssuer distribution point, the full name is the CRL issuer name with the relative name appended. Since the change that deferred this computation, crl_crldp_check() rebuilds that full name for each candidate CRL and frees it again.  CMS_verify() and PKCS7_verify() take both the distribution points and the candidate CRLs from the message, and this scoring runs before any signature is checked. An application is exposed only if it sets X509_V_FLAG_CRL_CHECK on the store and does not pass CMS_NOCRL or PKCS7_NOCRL; CRL checking is off by default. In TLS the CRLs come from the local store, so a peer controls only the distribution point count.  The cost grows with the product of the distribution point count, the CRL count and the issuer name length, all chosen by the message author; a few hundred kilobytes can occupy a CPU core for tens of seconds. Verification still fails as it should, with no crash, no incorrect result and no memory growth. Requiring CRL checking is what limits the severity.  FIPS impact: no The affected code is outside the FIPS module boundary.

title: openssl: openssl: Denial of Service via memory leak in QUIC stream handling

vendor.description: Issue summary: A QUIC server that rejects a stream opened by the peer may retain that stream's state for the lifetime of the connection if the peer resets the stream before the rejection is signalled, even though the peer's stream credit is returned.  Impact summary: A remote client that completes a QUIC handshake can repeatedly open and reset streams, causing server memory to grow without bound until the process runs out of memory and every connection on it is lost. This is a Denial of Service.  CWE: CWE-401: Missing Release of Memory after Effective Lifetime  Description: QUIC servers track each stream the peer opens. When the incoming stream policy rejects a stream, OpenSSL schedules a STOP_SENDING frame, marks the stream deleted and returns the peer's stream credit. A deleted stream is collected only once its receive part is fully drained, which for a rejected stream means the STOP_SENDING has been acknowledged. If the peer sends RESET_STREAM first, the reset cancels the pending STOP_SENDING, so it is never sent or acknowledged and the stream is never collected.  The default configuration reaches this path. Once a connection has a default stream, meaning the application has read from or written to the connection as the tutorial server does, the effective incoming stream policy rejects streams the application does not accept. Applications that set the REJECT policy explicitly are affected too.  Each retained stream costs about 300 bytes, and the peer's stream credit window paces how quickly they accumulate. A client that keeps the connection open and keeps opening and resetting streams grows server memory without bound. The severity is Low because growth is slow, needs a long-lived connection, and causes no memory corruption or disclosure.  FIPS impact: no The affected code is outside the FIPS module boundary.

title: openssl: openssl: Denial of Service via out-of-bounds read during TLS key-share processing

vendor.description: Issue summary: A server configured with the Suite B certificate flag through SSL_CTX_set_cert_flags() and with TLS 1.3 enabled may read past the end of a fixed group list when it processes a ClientHello whose supported_groups and key_share contain no Suite B group.  Impact summary: A remote client can send a ClientHello that makes the server read past the end of a static array. The values read are never returned to the client, so no memory is disclosed; on builds with sanitizers or hardened allocators the read may crash the process, causing Denial of Service.  CWE: CWE-125: Out-of-bounds Read  Description: When the Suite B certificate flag is set, OpenSSL restricts the accepted groups to P-256 and P-384 by substituting a fixed two-element list for the configured group list. The tuple machinery used for key-share selection was not updated for this substitution: tls1_get_group_tuples() still returns the configured tuples, which by default describe eight groups. The server-side walk in tls_parse_ctos_key_share() then advances through the two-element list using those tuple counts without checking the cumulative offset against the number of groups present.  Only applications that call SSL_CTX_set_cert_flags() with SSL_CERT_FLAG_SUITEB_128_LOS and leave TLS 1.3 enabled are affected. The openssl s_server -suiteB_128 option sets an X.509 verification parameter instead, so the stock command line server is not vulnerable. Default configurations do not reach this code.  A client that offers only groups outside the Suite B set, such as X25519, forces every tuple to be walked and the read to run past the array. The bytes read are compared against client group IDs and never sent back, so no memory is disclosed. On builds with address sanitizers or hardened allocators the read can abort the process; in ordinary release builds it reads a few bytes of adjacent constant data.  FIPS impact: no The affected code is outside the FIPS module boundary.

title: Issue summary: A QUIC peer that sends many small out-of-order STREAM f ...

vendor.description: Issue summary: A QUIC peer that sends many small out-of-order STREAM fragments while withholding the first byte of the stream may cause OpenSSL to buffer a large number of reassembly nodes occupying much larger memory than the actual data sent.  Impact summary: A remote peer can pin large amounts of memory on a server that accepts incoming QUIC streams, potentially exhausting memory and causing Denial of Service.  CWE: CWE-770: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling  Description: QUIC receive flow control limits the highest byte offset a peer may reach on a stream. It does not limit how many out-of-order fragments the receiver buffers. OpenSSL allocates a reassembly node for each non-adjacent STREAM fragment and never caps the count. A peer that opens a stream and sends many one-byte fragments at increasing offsets, while withholding the first byte, makes the receiver retain one node per fragment without delivering any data.  Only applications that accept incoming streams are exposed. With the default policy, which rejects peer-initiated streams, the stream is torn down before state accumulates. Because the read side never advances past the missing prefix, the flow control window never slides and the nodes stay pinned for the life of the connection.  The per-stream window bounds the highest offset, so the memory one stream can pin is finite, but it can reach tens of megabytes and, across many streams and connections, drive memory pressure and Denial of Service. The severity is limited because the exhaustion is bounded by flow control and requires a non-default configuration.  FIPS impact: no The affected code is outside the FIPS module boundary.

title: openssl: OpenSSL: Denial of Service via NULL pointer dereference during DANE TLSA record processing

vendor.description: Issue summary: A DANE-enabled TLS client may crash by dereferencing a NULL pointer when processing an unusual combination of certificate and TLSA records.  Impact summary: The impact is limited to a client crash (potential Denial of Service).  CWE: CWE-476: NULL Pointer Dereference  Description: A DANE-enabled TLS client that supports TLSA records with at least one of the PKIX-TA(0) or PKIX-EE(1) usages alongside the DANE-TA(2) usage may crash by dereferencing a NULL pointer if the server claims a trusted CA's certificate to be its end-entity certificate and has an unusual mix of associated TLSA records. For example, the Postfix MTA is not affected, while the Exim MTA does not at present use OpenSSL's DANE implementation.  Use of DANE in validation of RFC7250 raw public keys (RPKs) is also unaffected, as these only use DANE-EE(3) TLSA records.  Only applications that support combining the DANE PKI with a traditional PKI are potentially affected.  A DANE-enabled browser or similar, that uses OpenSSL's DANE API could be affected.  FIPS impact: no The DANE API is outside the FIPS module boundary.

title: openssl: openssl: Information disclosure via uninitialized memory in QUIC peer detection

vendor.description: Issue summary: QUIC, when performing automated peer detection, may allow uninitialized stack data to leak into the received address which is then used as the destination for outgoing packets. vendor.description: Issue summary: Setting an AES-GCM-SIV IV shorter than the expected nonce length via EVP_CipherInit_ex() may trigger a heap out-of-bounds read. Supplying a longer IV is silently truncated instead of rejected.  Impact summary: An application passing a caller-supplied IV of the wrong length may crash or read beyond its buffer. Because trailing IV bytes are ignored, an attacker who knows one message and tag may forge messages under a different IV. When the caller passes a shorter IV, the copy reads past the end of the caller's buffer; AddressSanitizer confirms a heap out-of-bounds read reached through EVP_CipherInit_ex() into ossl_aes_gcm_siv_init(). When the caller passes a longer IV, the implementation silently discards the trailing bytes instead of rejecting the length.  The truncation breaks the binding between the IV and the computed authentication tag. An attacker who has observed a message and its tag under one IV can produce a message and tag that verify under a different IV whose first bytes match, since the surplus bytes never influence the computation. The message itself is unchanged, so this is a failure of IV commitment rather than a classic existential forgery. title: python: Python: Privilege escalation due to insecure VPATH handling in Windows legacy installers

vendor.description: To allow builds of Python to be run from an in-tree layout (rather than an installed file layout), the VPATH variable is defined at build time and used to locate certain landmarks - specifically, Modules/setup.local. When this landmark is found relative to VPATH relative to the executable, Python assumes it is running in a source tree and generates a different default sys.path. This code remains in release builds, so that release-ready builds can be built in-tree.  On Windows, since builds are written to 'PCbuild/', the value of VPATH is set to '..\..', which results in a landmark of '..\..\Modules\setup.local'. This path is outside the install directory of Python, and may have different permissions, potentially allowing a low-privilege user to create the landmark and an alternative `Lib` folder that will be discovered by an otherwise restricted install.  Such a setup occurs with the legacy default install location for all users (in the now superseded EXE installer), due to how Windows allows all users to create folders in the root directory of their OS drive.  Our recommended mitigation on Windows is to migrate away from the legacy installer and use the new [Python install manager](https://www.python.org/downloads/latest/pymanager/) to install for the current user. Installs where the directory two levels above the Python installation directory have equivalent permissions are unaffected (in general, a per-user install cannot be modified at all by other users, removing any escalation of privilege risk, and could be directly modified by a privileged user, making the potential tampering irrelevant). Alternative mitigations might include preemptively creating and restricting access to a `Modules` directory. Be aware that only 3.13 and 3.14 will receive updated legacy installers - earlier fixes are only provided as sources.  Platforms other than Windows allow VPATH to be overridden, but as they don't usually use a separated directory in the build for binaries, are unlikely to have a landmark reference outside of the install directory.  The landmark detection involving VPATH is a fallback for when a more specific landmark - .\pybuilddir.txt - is absent, and was included for compatibility. Future releases of Python will no longer include the fallback, and so builds will need to generate or preserve the pybuilddir.txt file in order to work in-tree. This landmark file has been generated on Windows since 3.11, and on other platforms for longer.

title: python: Python: Information disclosure due to incorrect URL scheme matching

vendor.description: The HTTPPasswordMgr class in the urllib.request module, along with its subclasses HTTPPasswordMgrWithDefaultRealm and HTTPPasswordMgrWithPriorAuth, did not take the URL scheme into account when matching stored credentials against a requested URL. title: glibc: glibc: Denial of Service via memory allocation failure during regular expression processing

vendor.description: The regcomp and regexec functions in the GNU C Library version 2.3 to version 2.44 may read freed memory and free the same heap block twice when a memory allocation fails while a regular expression is compiled or matched.  The re_dfa_add_node (the NFA node table) and build_range_exp (bracket ranges) grow several arrays with consecutive realloc calls and store the new pointers only after all of them succeed.  When a later call fails, the pattern buffer keeps pointers to blocks that were already freed, and the error cleanup frees them again.  In regexec, the back-reference cache (match_ctx_add_entry) frees its array when a realloc fails but keeps the pointer, which is freed again on the error path.  An attacker does not need to supply a crafted regular expression: patterns large enough to grow these arrays are common.  The failure has to hit a specific allocation, though, so the issue can only be reached when the system is already under memory pressure.  An attacker who supplies the pattern or the subject string has little control over which allocation fails, so the expected impact is a crash of the process.  This issue affects all architectures and ABIs supported by the GNU C Library.

title: glibc: glibc: Memory corruption via out-of-bounds write in wide scanf functions

vendor.description: Calling the wide scanf family of functions (swscanf, fwscanf, wscanf, vswscanf, vfwscanf and vwscanf) with a %s or %[ conversion without the 'l' length modifier in the GNU C Library version 2.2 to version 2.44 writes an extra null byte one past the end of the destination array when the converted multibyte string and its terminating null byte exactly fill that array.  These conversions store each wide input character into the caller's char array as a multibyte sequence.  The conversion ends with the sequence that returns to the initial shift state, which also stores the terminating null byte, and the functions then append a second null byte.  A destination sized for the converted string and one terminator, as the C standard requires the caller to provide, is therefore written one byte past its end.  The out-of-bounds byte is always a null byte, which may corrupt adjacent data or crash the process.  An attacker who supplies the input can trigger the overflow with a string whose converted length exactly fills the destination.  The narrow scanf functions, the %ls and %l[ conversions into a wchar_t array, and the 'a' and 'm' allocation modifiers are not affected, and storing a wide scanf conversion into a narrow char array is uncommon.  This issue affects all architectures and ABIs supported by the GNU C Library.

title: glibc: glibc: Denial of Service via out-of-bounds read in CP949 character conversion

If //IGNORE is set on the destination encoding and this sequence is at the end of the input buffer, the decoder may then end up reading past the bounds of the input buffer. title: glibc: glibc: Denial of Service via double free in glob functions

vendor.description: The glob functions in the GNU C Library versions 2.44 and earlier may free the same heap block twice when a memory allocation fails while glob prepends the directory name to the names it matched. The allocation must fail after at least one name has been rewritten, so the issue can only be reached when the process is already close to its memory limit, for example under an address space limit (RLIMIT_AS) or on a 32-bit system.  The attacker needs control to make the result large enough to make the program or service run out of memory, either by controlling the glob pattern and having knowledge of the filesystem layout or through other means.  This issue affects all architectures and ABIs supported by the GNU C Library.

title: glibc: glibc: Arbitrary code execution via directory traversal in LANGUAGE environment variable

vendor.description: The gettext family of functions in the GNU C Library version 2.0 and later accept LANGUAGE environment variable entries that contain '/' or that are equal to "..", unless the program is setuid or setgid (AT_SECURE).  An attacker who can set LANGUAGE in the environment of a program that uses gettext can make it load a message catalog (.mo file) from an arbitrary location in the file system.  A crafted .mo file can crash the program through out-of-range offsets, or supply translations whose format directives do not match the arguments passed by the program.  That causes undefined behaviour in the printf family of functions and may allow arbitrary code execution with the privileges of the program.  The safety of message catalogs relies on them being installed in trusted, read-only locations, and the directory traversal bypasses this.  The fix for CVE-2014-0475 rejects ".." path components in locale names passed to setlocale or taken from the LC_ALL, LC_* and LANG environment variables.  gettext reads LANGUAGE directly and appends each colon-separated entry to the message catalog directory, so that fix did not cover LANGUAGE.  LANGUAGE is only used when the LC_MESSAGES locale is not "C", "C.<encoding>" or "POSIX", so the attacker must also be able to select another installed locale, for example through LANG or LC_ALL.  Exploitation also requires that the attacker can place the crafted file in a location readable by the target program, and that the environment crosses a trust boundary without the program running as AT_SECURE.  An example is an SSH server that accepts LANGUAGE and LANG from clients through the AcceptEnv directive and restricts an account to a forced command; the attacker may use this to escape the restriction.
